newsitem.title: CANADA: Dozens flee dense smoke in Toronto subway fire.
newsitem.headline: Dozens flee dense smoke in Toronto subway fire.

text.p: Dozens of people were treated for smoke inhalation on Wednesday night after smoke from a railyard fire engulfed two subway trains in Canada's largest city.
At least 75 people fled or were evacuated from the Donlands subway station shortly after 7:30 p.m. EDT (2330 GMT) as thick black smoke poured into the tunnels.

Fire and transit officials said no one was seriously hurt in the incident, although an estimated 40 people were treated at the scene for minor injuries, while 20 were taken to hospitals for further examination and treatment.
Officials said the injuries were not life-threatening and no one was trapped in the station or tunnels.
The fire was extinguished by 10 p.m. EDT (0200 GMT Thursday).
"The fire is out and our preliminary investigation has not found anybody down there," Toronto Fire Chief Peter Ferguson told reporters at the scene.
Toronto Transit Commision (TTC) spokeswoman Marilyn Bolton said "a few people needed oxygen."

Denis Callan, the transit system's acting chief general manager, said the fire appeared to have started in a stack of rubber pads stored above ground. The smoke was then drawn into a tunnel leading to the Bloor-Danforth subway line, which runs east-west across the city.

Eyewitnesses said they fled the Donlands station after transit officials broadcast a message over loudspeakers ordering an evacuation. Several passengers emerged from the station with soot covering their faces, clothes and bodies.
"We could see the thick, black smoke and everyone tried to get up the stairs," one man said.

Others complained that they were forced to grope their way through the acrid smoke and darkened tunnels to find their own way out of the subway. Several emerged from another station near the Donlands stop.
"It was scary. Thick black smoke -- just like the movies," another passenger said.

Officials said 11 stations on the Bloor-Danforth line were closed as a result of the fire and smoke, as were several streets near the subway stops. For more than an hour after the incident began, smoke could be seen streaming from subway tunnel vents into the twilight sky.
Callan said officials were trying to determine the extent of smoke damage to the stations. "What we're trying to assess now is whether we can get service back for tomorrow morning," Callan said.

It was the second major mishap in the city's transit system in two years. In mid-August of 1995, a subway train ran into the back of a stationary train in a midtown station, killing three people and injuring 36 others.
The 1995 accident provoked an Ontario provincial government inquiry into what was once dubbed the world's safest transit system.
The subway serves 1.3 million passengers a day.
